newsitem.title: SPAIN: Defiant Spain reasserts claim to Gibraltar.
newsitem.headline: Defiant Spain reasserts claim to Gibraltar.

text.p: Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar declared Spain would never renounce its claim to Gibraltar on Wednesday, defying a British threat to block Madrid's full integration into NATO over the disputed colony.
British Foreign Secretary Robin Cook demanded on Tuesday that Spain lift air and sea restrictions on Gibraltar or face a veto to joining NATO's military command structure.

"The Spanish claim to Gibraltar is not renounceable and the integration of Spain into the NATO military structure will not affect this claim," Aznar told reporters at the close of the two-day NATO summit in Madrid.

The acrimonious exchange over Gibraltar cast a pall over Spain's attempt to show solidarity with NATO allies while hosting the historic summit where former communist enemies were invited to join for the first time.
Cook said that if Spain wanted to play a full role in NATO's integrated command structure, it must behave as an ally when British military aircraft went in and out of Gibraltar.
Spanish Foreign Minister Abel Matutes lashed back, vowing on Tuesday not to budge.
"Spain is not going to lift any restriction which could affect its legitimate demands of sovereignty over Gibraltar," Matutes said.

Spain claims sovereignty over the colony passed to Spanish hands in 1462 and seized by Britain in 1704. The rocky peninsula at the southern tip of Spain dominates the western entrance to the Mediterranean.

Gibraltar was ceded by Spain in perpetuity under the 1713 Treaty of Utrecht and became a British colony. Spain has claimed it ever since, and in particular the isthmus linking the rock to the mainland where the airstrip is located.
Aznar said Spain would not put anything on the negotiating table which jeopardised its claim to sovereignty over Gibraltar.

Aznar opened the summit on Tuesday morning by pledging to join NATO's military command in the near future, a signal that his country was setting aside historical ambivalence toward the Western military alliance.
Spain joined NATO in 1982 but a strong pacifist tradition made it difficult to fully embrace the organisation so it stayed out of the military command structure.
In November, parliament voted to participate in the military command but stipulated the country must remain free of nuclear weapons.
